sweep_summary: Anaang (anaa1238) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Urua & Udoh 2017 'The prosodic status of glides in Anaañ reduplication' (Benjamins LFAB 14, pp. 298-319; correct DOI 10.1075/lfab.14.c17 -- Glottolog's DOI is malformed), is paywalled: Unpaywall, CORE, OpenAIRE and Semantic Scholar show no open copy, benjamins.com blocks with not reachable by automated download; the abstract (downloaded from jbe-platform.com and saved) concerns the moraic status of glides and the heavy-light trochee of the reduplicant, not word-stress placement, so relevance is prosody-but-not-word-stress and acquisition priority is low. The best first-hand stress statements for Anaang are already held by the project from the prior search and were re-read here: Idem 1994 (Edinburgh PhD) p. 227 -- stress in Anaang is limited to emphasis/contrast/emotion, tone is the primary suprasegmental -- and Michael 2009 (Ibadan PhD) p. 97 -- all syllables carry the same strength, no reduced vowels, tone on every syllable (page image verified). Both agree: tone language, no lexical word stress. only API lookups were possible.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Anaang is a register tone language (H, L, downstepped H; restricted LH/HL contours) with a tone on every syllable; there is no word-level stress: all syllables of a word are produced with equal strength and there are no reduced vowels. Independently, Idem (1994: 227) states that stress in Anaang functions only for emphasis, contrast and emotion, tone being the primary suprasegmental.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; source explicitly denies any syllable-strength asymmetry within the word.
new_statements.exceptions: None in Michael 2009. Idem 1994 (p. 227) allows stress only as an utterance-level device for emphasis/contrast/emotion (after Essien 1990 on Ibibio).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the word (contrast with English lexical primary stress) and is made in a loanword-adaptation section; the equal-strength claim is attributed to Udoh 1998 (Calabar PhD, not accessible). Corroborated first-hand by Idem 1994 sect. 6.2.2.4 (Edinburgh PhD, also saved) and by Ighile & Michael 2013 ('Anaang.. is syllable-timed and tonal').
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe Anaang in general (anaa1238), by native-speaker linguists; Michael 2009 used 12 speakers and does not restrict to one dialect in the pages read; Akpabio et al. 2021 tone data are from Abak LGA. No sub-dialect glottocodes involved. Closely related Ibibio (ibib1240) and Efik (efik1245) are explicitly said by Idem 1994 to behave the same way.

new_statements.quote: While stress plays a major role in English as indicated in section 6.2.1.4, its functions in Anaang (as in Ibibio and Efik) are limited to the expression of emphasis, contrast and emotion (irritation, anger, frustration or desperation) (Essien, 1990). In the same vein, intonation plays a minor role in the language serving only certain syntactic/semantic functions such as the expression of modality - the speaker's attitude or involvement in what he/she says. Tone, on the contrary, constitutes the most important suprasegmental feature in Anaang phonology. The basic tones are "high" and "low"
new_statements.citation: Idem, Unyierie Angela Walter. 1994. Phonological processes in the acquisition of liquid and stop segments in English by Anaang speakers. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh.
new_statements.reading: Anaang has no word-level (lexical) stress: prominence is used only pragmatically for emphasis, contrast and emotion; the language is a tone language (H, L, falling, rising, downstep). Corroborated independently by Michael 2009 p. 97 ('all syllables in Anaang carry the same strength (Udoh 1998) since there is no reduced vowel in Anaang'). If Anaang were added to the catalog it would be coded as a tone language without word stress (no fixed or lexical stress position).

sources.quote: With reduplication as a basis, this paper employs correspondence theory to examine the precise pre-peak and post-peak positions of glides in the Anaañ syllable, with a view to ascertaining their moraic status and place in the verbal foot construction. [...] It was discovered that the pre-peak glide in Anaañ (with no mora value) belongs to the nucleus, since it remains undeleted in the reduplicant (RED) morpheme. Contrary to CV inputs, where the no-single-mora constraint comes out as emergently unmarked, the glide in CGV inputs is analysed as the normal application of lengthening in RED, to maintain a minimally permitted heavy-light trochee.
sources.locator: abstract (JBE platform landing page, chapter pp. 298-319)
sources.note: Abstract says nothing about where word stress falls. It is a correspondence-theory analysis of the moraic status of on-glides and off-glides in Anaañ verbal reduplication (RED is a heavy-light trochee; CV bases lengthen in RED; off-glide vs true-consonant deletion by sonority vs NOCODA).
